case.name: OKIRIKA
case.summary: A hotter, deeper, saltier sand (90 degC, 34 MPa, 80000 ppm, gas 0.75, 30 API at 90 L/L) with a quartz, calcite and clay frame, logged in brine at 3520/2050/2310 under a 2900/1450/2480 shale, on a 30 Hz survey.

literals_ok.1: the 1 ms sample grid of the wedge model

beginner.prompt: The OKIRIKA sand sits at 90 degC and 34 MPa, with a brine of 80000 ppm NaCl. What brine density does the engine return there?
beginner.correct: {{b_brine_rho}} kg/m3, with the salinity entered as a weight fraction of 0.08
distractors: {{b_brine_rho_slip}} kg/m3, which is what comes back once 80000 ppm is typed as 0.008
{{b_water_rho}} kg/m3, the pure water density at those conditions with the salt term dropped
{{b_brine_rho_surface}} kg/m3, the same brine read at 20 degC and surface pressure
beginner.explanation: The engine takes salinity as a weight fraction, so 80000 ppm is 0.08, and at 90 degC and 34 MPa that brine is {{b_brine_rho}} kg/m3. The same brine at the surface reads {{b_brine_rho_surface}} kg/m3, which is why a density must carry its conditions.
why_wrong: salinity typed ten times too small
surface conditions instead of in situ

beginner.prompt: The OKIRIKA brine is 0.08 NaCl by weight at 90 degC and 34 MPa. Which bulk modulus belongs on its fluid sheet?
beginner.correct: {{b_brine_k_gpa}} GPa, the in situ value at the stated temperature and pressure
distractors: {{b_brine_k_surface_gpa}} GPa, the laboratory value measured at 20 degC and surface pressure
{{b_brine_k_slip_gpa}} GPa, from the salinity typed ten times too small as 0.008
{{b_brine_k_low_salt_gpa}} GPa, the modulus of the same brine at a salinity of 0.01
beginner.explanation: Batzle-Wang at 90 degC, 34 MPa and 0.08 gives {{b_brine_k_gpa}} GPa. Every other figure is the same engine at the wrong temperature or salinity, and nothing in the number itself would say so.

beginner.prompt: The OKIRIKA gas has a gravity of 0.75 at 90 degC and 34 MPa. Which bulk modulus should the fluid sheet carry for it?
beginner.correct: {{b_gas_k_mpa}} MPa, from the Batzle-Wang gas relations at the stated gravity
distractors: {{b_gas_k_light_mpa}} MPa, the value for a 0.6 gravity gas at the same conditions
{{b_gas_k_isothermal_mpa}} MPa, since a slowly compressed ideal gas has a modulus equal to its pressure
{{b_gas_k_halfp_mpa}} MPa, the modulus this gas would have at half the pore pressure
beginner.explanation: At 0.75 gravity, 90 degC and 34 MPa the engine gives {{b_gas_k_mpa}} MPa. The isothermal ideal gas figure of 34 MPa ignores both the adiabatic response and the real gas behaviour the correlation carries.
why_wrong: default gravity instead of the stated one

beginner.prompt: By bulk modulus, how many times stiffer than the OKIRIKA gas is the OKIRIKA brine?
beginner.correct: {{b_stiff_ratio}} times, the ratio of {{b_brine_k_gpa}} GPa to {{b_gas_k_mpa}} MPa
distractors: {{b_rho_ratio}} times, which is the ratio of the two fluid densities
{{b_vp_ratio}} times, which is the ratio of their compressional velocities
{{b_stiff_ratio_iso}} times, taking the gas modulus as equal to its 34 MPa pressure
beginner.explanation: {{b_brine_k_gpa}} GPa over {{b_gas_k_mpa}} MPa is {{b_stiff_ratio}}, once both are in the same unit. The density ratio is only {{b_rho_ratio}}, which is why gas moves stiffness far more than density.

beginner.prompt: The OKIRIKA oil is 30 API with a gas oil ratio of 90 L/L and a 0.75 gravity solution gas. What in situ density belongs on the sheet?
beginner.correct: {{b_oil_rho}} kg/m3, the live oil with its dissolved gas at 90 degC and 34 MPa
distractors: {{b_rho0}} kg/m3, the stock tank density that 30 API converts to
{{b_dead_rho}} kg/m3, the gas free oil at the same temperature and pressure
{{b_oil_rho_light_gas}} kg/m3, the live oil worked with a 0.6 gravity solution gas
beginner.explanation: Dissolved gas swells the oil, so the live oil at 90 L/L is {{b_oil_rho}} kg/m3 against {{b_dead_rho}} kg/m3 for the dead oil and {{b_rho0}} kg/m3 at stock tank.

beginner.prompt: The OKIRIKA frame is 0.62 quartz, 0.2 calcite and 0.18 clay by volume. What Voigt Reuss Hill bulk modulus does the engine give it?
beginner.correct: {{b_frame_k_gpa}} GPa, the mean of the Voigt and Reuss bounds
distractors: {{b_k_voigt_gpa}} GPa, the volume weighted average of the three moduli
{{b_k_reuss_gpa}} GPa, the harmonic average of the three mineral moduli
{{b_frame_k_nocalcite_gpa}} GPa, the same frame with the calcite counted as quartz
beginner.explanation: Voigt gives {{b_k_voigt_gpa}} GPa and Reuss {{b_k_reuss_gpa}} GPa, and their mean is {{b_frame_k_gpa}} GPa. Counting the calcite as quartz drops the value to {{b_frame_k_nocalcite_gpa}} GPa, because calcite is the stiffest mineral in the mix.

beginner.prompt: On the OKIRIKA frame, how far apart do the Voigt and Reuss bounds sit for the bulk modulus and for the shear modulus?
beginner.correct: About {{b_k_spread_pct}} percent for bulk and {{b_mu_spread_pct}} percent for shear, so shear is the weaker claim
distractors: About {{b_mu_spread_pct}} percent for bulk and {{b_k_spread_pct}} percent for shear, so bulk is the weaker claim
About {{b_k_spread_pct}} percent for both, since the same volume fractions weight both averages
Under a percent for both, since calcite and quartz lie close together in every modulus
beginner.explanation: Voigt over Reuss is {{b_k_voigt_gpa}} over {{b_k_reuss_gpa}} GPa for bulk and {{b_mu_voigt_gpa}} over {{b_mu_reuss_gpa}} GPa for shear. The soft clay pulls the shear Reuss bound down hard, so the shear VRH value is the looser claim.
why_wrong: the spread depends on the moduli and not only the fractions
calcite is far stiffer than quartz in bulk and softer in shear

beginner.prompt: The OKIRIKA frame has VRH moduli of {{b_frame_k_gpa}} GPa bulk and {{b_frame_mu_gpa}} GPa shear, and a density of {{b_frame_rho}} kg/m3. What compressional velocity would the solid mineral carry?
beginner.correct: {{b_frame_vp}} m/s, the square root of K plus four thirds of mu, over density
distractors: {{b_frame_vp_noshear}} m/s, the square root of the bulk modulus over density alone
{{b_frame_vp_kmu}} m/s, adding the whole shear modulus to the bulk modulus
{{b_frame_vs}} m/s, the square root of the shear modulus over density
beginner.explanation: A compressional wave works against both the bulk modulus and four thirds of the shear modulus, which gives {{b_frame_vp}} m/s. Leaving the shear out gives only {{b_frame_vp_noshear}} m/s.

beginner.prompt: The OKIRIKA pore fluid is mixed at Sw 0.9, with the rest gas. What bulk modulus does Wood's equation give for the mix?
beginner.correct: {{b_mix_k_mpa}} MPa, a harmonic average that the soft gas dominates
distractors: {{b_mix_k_linear_mpa}} MPa, the saturation weighted linear average of the two
{{b_mix_k_hill_mpa}} MPa, the mean of the linear and harmonic averages
{{b_mix_k_swapped_mpa}} MPa, from the mix with the two saturations exchanged
beginner.explanation: Wood's equation adds compliances, so the mix at Sw 0.9 is {{b_mix_k_mpa}} MPa, far below the {{b_mix_k_linear_mpa}} MPa a linear average would give.

beginner.prompt: At Sw 0.9 in the OKIRIKA sand, what density does the mixed brine and gas pore fluid carry?
beginner.correct: {{b_mix_rho}} kg/m3, the saturation weighted sum of the two
distractors: {{b_mix_rho_harm}} kg/m3, a harmonic average in the same way as the modulus
{{b_mix_rho_swapped}} kg/m3, the weighted sum with the saturations exchanged
{{b_brine_rho}} kg/m3, since that little gas cannot move the density
beginner.explanation: Density mixes linearly: 0.9 of {{b_brine_rho}} plus the rest of {{b_gas_rho}} is {{b_mix_rho}} kg/m3, only {{b_mix_rho_drop_pct}} percent below the brine.
why_wrong: harmonic mixing applies to moduli only

beginner.prompt: In the OKIRIKA mix at Sw 0.9, what share of the total compliance does the gas term carry?
beginner.correct: {{b_gas_compliance_pct}} percent, though the gas fills a tenth of the pore volume
distractors: {{b_brine_compliance_pct}} percent, since the brine fills most of the pore volume
{{b_mix_k_drop_pct}} percent, the fall in bulk modulus from the pure brine value
{{b_mix_rho_drop_pct}} percent, the fall in density from the pure brine value
beginner.explanation: The gas term is its saturation over {{b_gas_k_mpa}} MPa, which carries {{b_gas_compliance_pct}} percent of the total, so a tenth of the pore volume does most of the softening.
why_wrong: answers a different question: modulus drop
answers a different question: density drop

beginner.prompt: The OKIRIKA pore pressure is 34 MPa. In a depleted block of the same field at 17 MPa, how would the gas bulk modulus compare?
beginner.correct: {{b_gas_k_halfp_mpa}} MPa, so the undepleted gas at 34 MPa is {{b_gas_k_p_ratio}} times stiffer
distractors: Half of {{b_gas_k_mpa}} MPa, since the modulus scales in proportion with pressure
{{b_gas_k_mpa}} MPa, since a gas modulus is set by temperature and gravity alone
About {{b_gas_rho_p_ratio}} times lower, the factor by which the gas density falls
beginner.explanation: The engine gives {{b_gas_k_halfp_mpa}} MPa at 17 MPa against {{b_gas_k_mpa}} MPa at 34 MPa, a factor of {{b_gas_k_p_ratio}}. The modulus falls faster than pressure, and faster than the density, which drops by {{b_gas_rho_p_ratio}}.
why_wrong: modulus does not scale linearly with pressure
density ratio is not the modulus ratio

beginner.prompt: The OKIRIKA brine is 0.08 NaCl by weight. How much stiffer is it than the same brine at 0.01, at the same 90 degC and 34 MPa?
beginner.correct: {{b_salt_k_rise_pct}} percent stiffer, {{b_brine_k_gpa}} GPa at 0.08 against {{b_brine_k_low_salt_gpa}} GPa at 0.01
distractors: About eight times as stiff, since the salinity is eight times higher and the modulus follows
No stiffer at all, since salt adds mass to the brine and leaves its modulus alone
{{b_salt_rho_rise}} kg/m3 denser and no stiffer, since salt only adds mass to the water
beginner.explanation: Raising the salinity from 0.01 to 0.08 raises the modulus from {{b_brine_k_low_salt_gpa}} to {{b_brine_k_gpa}} GPa, {{b_salt_k_rise_pct}} percent, and the density by {{b_salt_rho_rise}} kg/m3. Salt stiffens the brine as well as weighting it.
why_wrong: modulus is not proportional to salinity
salt raises the velocity and the modulus
salt raises the velocity and the modulus

beginner.prompt: An OKIRIKA fluid sheet lists the Sw 0.9 mixed fluid at {{b_mix_k_linear_mpa}} MPa. What does a quality check say about it?
beginner.correct: It was averaged linearly; Wood's equation gives {{b_mix_k_mpa}} MPa, near the gas end
distractors: It passes, since {{b_mix_k_linear_mpa}} MPa lies between the gas and brine moduli as it must
The saturations were exchanged, and the correct mixed value is {{b_mix_k_swapped_mpa}} MPa
The gas was entered in GPa, and the correct gas modulus is {{b_gas_k_mpa}} MPa
beginner.explanation: A Wood mix must sit near the soft end: {{b_mix_k_mpa}} MPa between {{b_gas_k_mpa}} MPa and {{b_brine_k_gpa}} GPa. A value near the middle is the linear average, the error the harmonic check exists for.
why_wrong: lying between the end members is not enough
a GPa slip would be off by a thousand

intermediate.prompt: The OKIRIKA sand is logged in brine at vp 3520 m/s, vs 2050 m/s and 2310 kg/m3. What saturated bulk modulus goes into inverse Gassmann?
intermediate.correct: {{i_ksat_gpa}} GPa, rho vp squared less four thirds of the shear modulus
distractors: {{i_rhovp2_gpa}} GPa, rho vp squared, which is the full compressional modulus
{{i_rho_vp2_minus_vs2_gpa}} GPa, rho times the difference of the squared velocities
{{i_mu_gpa}} GPa, rho vs squared, which the log gives directly
intermediate.explanation: The shear modulus is 2310 times 2050 squared, {{i_mu_gpa}} GPa, and the saturated bulk modulus is rho vp squared less four thirds of it, {{i_ksat_gpa}} GPa.
why_wrong: subtracts mu once instead of four thirds

intermediate.prompt: For the OKIRIKA log point take porosity 0.2, a mineral modulus of {{i_kmin_gpa}} GPa and the brine at {{b_brine_k_gpa}} GPa. What dry frame modulus does inverse Gassmann recover?
intermediate.correct: {{i_kdry_gpa}} GPa, with the brine removed from the logged saturated modulus
distractors: {{i_kdry_asgas_gpa}} GPa, from treating the logged interval as gas bearing
{{i_ksat_gpa}} GPa, the saturated modulus, since brine adds no stiffness
{{i_kmin_gpa}} GPa, the mineral frame modulus from the VRH average
intermediate.explanation: Inverse Gassmann takes the {{i_ksat_gpa}} GPa saturated modulus and strips the brine, leaving {{i_kdry_gpa}} GPa. The dry frame is the porous rock with empty pores, far softer than the {{i_kmin_gpa}} GPa mineral.
why_wrong: wrong fluid state for the log
mineral frame is not the dry frame

intermediate.prompt: What Biot coefficient does the recovered OKIRIKA dry frame imply, and what does it say about the substitution?
intermediate.correct: {{i_biot}}, so the sand should respond strongly to its pore fluid
distractors: {{i_biot}}, so the sand should be almost blind to its pore fluid
{{i_biot_ksat}}, from the saturated modulus over the mineral modulus instead
{{i_biot_mu}}, from the ratio of the rock and mineral shear moduli taken instead
intermediate.explanation: One minus {{i_kdry_gpa}} over {{i_kmin_gpa}} GPa is {{i_biot}}. Near one the fluid matters greatly, so a large gas effect is expected here.
why_wrong: a coefficient near one means fluid sensitive
Biot is a bulk modulus ratio

intermediate.prompt: Replace the OKIRIKA brine with the gas ({{b_gas_k_mpa}} MPa, {{b_gas_rho}} kg/m3) at porosity 0.2. What compressional velocity does Gassmann predict?
intermediate.correct: {{i_gas_vp}} m/s, with the new bulk modulus and the lighter density
distractors: {{i_gas_vp_rhofixed}} m/s, with the density left at the logged brine value of 2310 kg/m3
{{i_gas_vp_quartz_kmin}} m/s, with the {{i_kmin_quartz_gpa}} GPa of pure quartz as mineral
{{i_oil_vp}} m/s, which is the Gassmann result for the live OKIRIKA oil
intermediate.explanation: Forward Gassmann gives {{i_gas_ksat_gpa}} GPa, the shear modulus stays {{i_mu_gpa}} GPa and the density falls to {{i_gas_rho}} kg/m3, so vp is {{i_gas_vp}} m/s.

intermediate.prompt: After the OKIRIKA brine to gas substitution, what shear velocity should the gas case carry?
intermediate.correct: {{i_gas_vs}} m/s, above the log because the density fell
distractors: {{i_gas_vs_rhofixed}} m/s, unchanged since shear is blind to the fluid
{{i_gas_vs_rho_up}} m/s, below the log since the density rose
{{i_gas_vs_mudrock}} m/s, from the mudrock line on the gas case vp
intermediate.explanation: The shear modulus stays {{i_mu_gpa}} GPa and the density falls to {{i_gas_rho}} kg/m3, so vs rises to {{i_gas_vs}} m/s.
why_wrong: the modulus is blind, the velocity is not

intermediate.prompt: What bulk density does the OKIRIKA sand carry once its pores hold the gas ({{b_gas_rho}} kg/m3) in place of the brine ({{b_brine_rho}} kg/m3)?
intermediate.correct: {{i_gas_rho}} kg/m3, the log less 0.2 times the brine to gas density difference
distractors: {{i_gas_rho_graingas}} kg/m3, treating the logged density as the grain density
{{i_gas_rho_up}} kg/m3, the log plus 0.2 times the density difference
2310 kg/m3, since Gassmann changes the moduli and leaves density alone
intermediate.explanation: Only the pore fraction changes fluid: 2310 less 0.2 times the difference of {{b_brine_rho}} and {{b_gas_rho}} is {{i_gas_rho}} kg/m3.
why_wrong: the log already holds pore fluid

intermediate.prompt: By how much does the acoustic impedance of the OKIRIKA sand fall from the logged brine case to full gas?
intermediate.correct: {{i_z_drop_pct}} percent, from {{i_z_brine_e6}} to {{i_z_gas_e6}} million in SI units
distractors: {{i_vp_drop_pct}} percent, the fall in compressional velocity on its own
{{i_rho_drop_pct}} percent, the fall in bulk density on its own
{{i_vpvs_drop_pct}} percent, the fall in the ratio of vp to vs
intermediate.explanation: Impedance is density times vp, and both fall, so it drops {{i_z_drop_pct}} percent, more than either the {{i_vp_drop_pct}} percent in vp or the {{i_rho_drop_pct}} percent in density.
why_wrong: vp over vs is a different attribute

intermediate.prompt: If the OKIRIKA pores held the live oil ({{b_oil_k_gpa}} GPa, {{b_oil_rho}} kg/m3) in place of brine, what vp would Gassmann predict?
intermediate.correct: {{i_oil_vp}} m/s, only {{i_oil_gas_sep}} m/s above the full gas case
distractors: {{i_dead_vp}} m/s, which is the result for the gas free oil
{{i_gas_vp}} m/s, as for gas, since every hydrocarbon softens alike
3520 m/s, since the oil is too stiff to move the logged velocity
intermediate.explanation: The live oil gives {{i_oil_vp}} m/s against {{i_gas_vp}} m/s for gas, a separation of {{i_oil_gas_sep}} m/s, smaller than the {{i_phi_range_ms}} m/s a porosity error of 0.05 can make.
why_wrong: dead oil is stiffer than live oil

intermediate.prompt: In the OKIRIKA sand, what share of the whole brine to gas vp drop has already happened at Sw 0.99?
intermediate.correct: {{i_first_pct_share}} percent, with vp already down to {{i_vp_sw99}} m/s
distractors: About one percent, in proportion to the gas saturation reached
{{i_sw90_share}} percent, which is the share reached by Sw 0.9
About half, since vp falls in a straight line with saturation
intermediate.explanation: At Sw 0.99 vp is {{i_vp_sw99}} m/s, which is {{i_first_pct_share}} percent of the way from 3520 to the {{i_gas_vp}} m/s full gas case: the first percent of gas does a quarter of the work.

intermediate.prompt: Scanning the OKIRIKA sand from full brine to full gas in steps of 0.01, where is vp lowest?
intermediate.correct: At Sw {{i_vpmin_sw}}, {{i_vpmin}} m/s, which is {{i_vpmin_below_gas}} m/s below the full gas case
distractors: At full gas, {{i_gas_vp}} m/s, since vp keeps falling as gas replaces brine
At Sw 0.99, {{i_vp_sw99}} m/s, since the first percent of gas does the work
At Sw 0.9, {{i_vp_sw90}} m/s, where the density term first overtakes the modulus
intermediate.explanation: Once the fluid modulus has collapsed, more gas only lightens the rock and vp recovers, so the minimum of {{i_vpmin}} m/s sits at Sw {{i_vpmin_sw}}, below the full gas {{i_gas_vp}} m/s.
why_wrong: vp recovers at high gas saturation

intermediate.prompt: The OKIRIKA porosity is 0.2 with an uncertainty of 0.05 either way. What range does that put on the full gas vp?
intermediate.correct: {{i_gas_vp_phi_lo}} m/s at 0.15 up to {{i_gas_vp_phi_hi}} m/s at 0.25, a spread of {{i_phi_range_ms}} m/s
distractors: {{i_gas_vp_phi_hi}} m/s at 0.15 down to {{i_gas_vp_phi_lo}} m/s at 0.25, since more pore space holds more gas
None, since the porosity cancels between inverse and forward Gassmann
A spread of {{i_oil_gas_sep}} m/s, the same as the separation between oil and gas
intermediate.explanation: The dry frame is recovered with the porosity, so a lower porosity gives a softer frame and a lower gas vp: {{i_gas_vp_phi_lo}} m/s at 0.15 and {{i_gas_vp_phi_hi}} m/s at 0.25.

intermediate.prompt: An OKIRIKA interval has vp 3350 m/s, no shear log and a sandstone to shale split of 0.8 and 0.2. What vs does Greenberg-Castagna give?
intermediate.correct: {{i_gc_vs}} m/s, the mean of the arithmetic and harmonic averages
distractors: {{i_mudrock_vs}} m/s, from the Castagna mudrock line
{{i_gc_sand_vs}} m/s, from the sandstone regression taken alone
{{i_gc_shale_vs}} m/s, from the shale regression taken alone
intermediate.explanation: The sandstone and shale regressions give {{i_gc_sand_vs}} and {{i_gc_shale_vs}} m/s, and averaging their arithmetic and harmonic means at 0.8 and 0.2 gives {{i_gc_vs}} m/s.

intermediate.prompt: Test the same estimator at the logged OKIRIKA brine point, vp 3520 m/s, where vs was measured at 2050 m/s. What does the test show?
intermediate.correct: {{i_gc_at_log}} m/s, an error of {{i_gc_at_log_err_pct}} percent against the measured shear
distractors: Exactly 2050 m/s, since the regression is fitted to this well
{{i_mudrock_at_log}} m/s, since the mudrock line is the estimator under test
{{i_gc_at_gas_vp}} m/s, run on the gas case vp after substitution
intermediate.explanation: Greenberg-Castagna at 3520 m/s gives {{i_gc_at_log}} m/s, {{i_gc_at_log_err_pct}} percent against the log. Run on the gas case vp it gives {{i_gc_at_gas_vp}} m/s, {{i_gc_at_gas_err_pct}} percent low, which is why shear is estimated on brine first.
why_wrong: regression is published, not fitted here
must run on the brine case

intermediate.prompt: As a check on the assumed porosity of 0.2, what grain density does the OKIRIKA brine log point imply?
intermediate.correct: {{i_grain_rho}} kg/m3, close to the {{b_frame_rho}} kg/m3 of the mineral mix
distractors: {{i_grain_rho_gas}} kg/m3, taking the gas density as the pore fluid
{{i_grain_rho_nofluid}} kg/m3, the bulk density over one minus porosity
{{b_frame_rho}} kg/m3 exactly, since the log must return the mineral density
intermediate.explanation: Grain density is 2310 less 0.2 times {{b_brine_rho}}, over 0.8, which is {{i_grain_rho}} kg/m3, within a percent of the {{b_frame_rho}} kg/m3 frame. The porosity is consistent with the rock.
why_wrong: an independent check need not be exact

advanced.prompt: Put the OKIRIKA shale (vp 2800 m/s, vs 1560 m/s, 2500 kg/m3) over the brine sand (vp 3520 m/s, vs 2050 m/s and 2310 kg/m3). What is the normal incidence reflection coefficient?
distractors: {{a_ni_brine_flip}}, with the two rocks taken the other way up
{{a_vp_only_brine}}, from the velocity contrast alone
{{a_rho_only_brine}}, from the density contrast alone
advanced.explanation: The sand impedance is {{i_z_brine_e6}} million against the shale's lower value, so the coefficient is {{a_ni_brine}}. The density contrast alone is negative, and the velocity wins.

advanced.prompt: Under the OKIRIKA shale, what happens to the normal incidence reflection when the sand's brine is replaced by gas?
advanced.correct: It flips sign, from {{a_ni_brine}} for brine to {{a_ni_gas}} for gas
distractors: It keeps its sign and grows, since gas raises the sand's shear velocity
It stays positive and dims, since gas changes only the sand density
It goes to zero, since the shale and gas sand impedances match
advanced.explanation: The gas sand impedance of {{i_z_gas_e6}} million falls below the shale's, so the coefficient goes from {{a_ni_brine}} to {{a_ni_gas}}.

advanced.prompt: What Shuey intercept A and gradient B does the OKIRIKA shale over the brine sand give?
advanced.correct: A {{a_A_brine}} and B {{a_B_brine}}, from the logged brine sand
distractors: A {{a_A_brine_transposed}} and B {{a_B_brine_transposed}}, rocks transposed
A {{a_A_gas}} and B {{a_B_gas}}, which belong to the gas twin
A {{a_A_brine_vponly}} and B {{a_B_brine}}, the intercept from vp alone
advanced.explanation: Shuey on the shale over the brine sand gives A {{a_A_brine}}, within a thousandth of the normal incidence {{a_ni_brine}}, and B {{a_B_brine}}.

advanced.prompt: At a class threshold of 0.02, which Rutherford-Williams classes do the OKIRIKA brine and gas cases fall in?
advanced.correct: Brine class I and gas class II, since the gas intercept sits inside the band
distractors: Brine class I and gas class III, since the intercept changes sign once gas is in
Brine class II and gas class III, since both intercepts are small
Both class I, since the gas intercept is too small to count
advanced.explanation: The brine intercept {{a_A_brine}} is above 0.02, class I. The gas intercept {{a_A_gas}} is negative but inside the 0.02 band, so it is class II even though the sign flipped.
why_wrong: the band decides, and the sign alone does not
the brine intercept is well above 0.02
a negative intercept cannot be class I

advanced.prompt: How robust is the OKIRIKA gas class II call to the choice of class threshold?
advanced.correct: Fragile: its intercept is {{a_gas_A_over_thresh}} of the 0.02 band, and at 0.01 it becomes class III
distractors: Robust: it stays class II at every threshold chosen, since its gradient is negative
Fragile: at 0.01 it becomes class IV, since its gradient is negative
Robust: it would only leave class II above a threshold of 0.05
advanced.explanation: The gas intercept {{a_A_gas}} is {{a_gas_A_over_thresh}} of the 0.02 threshold, so a threshold of 0.01 makes it class III. The brine call, at {{a_brine_A_over_thresh}} times the threshold, holds at 0.05.
why_wrong: the class moves with the threshold
class IV needs a positive gradient
a higher threshold keeps it class II

advanced.prompt: Split the OKIRIKA gas case gradient into its vp, density and shear terms. Which one drives it?
advanced.correct: The shear term, {{a_Bg_vs_term}}, against {{a_Bg_vp_term}} for vp and {{a_Bg_rho_term}} for density
distractors: The density term, since replacing brine with gas lowers the density
The vp term, since replacing brine with gas lowers vp the most
All three about equally, each near a third of the total {{a_B_gas}}
